chapters.title: Ravana as Devotee — The Paradox of the Learned Sinner

verses.sanskrit: शिवमेकं शरण्यं च सर्वज्ञं सर्वकारणम् | रावणः प्रणिपत्याह शिवस्तोत्रमनुत्तमम् ||
verses.transliteration: śivamEkaṃ śaraṇyaṃ ca sarvajñaṃ sarvakāraṇam | rāvaṇaḥ praṇipatyāha śivastotramAnuttamam ||
verses.translation: Shiva alone — the refuge, the all-knowing, the cause of all. Ravana, having bowed completely, spoke the supreme hymn to Shiva.
verses.hindi: शिव को ही एकमात्र शरण, सर्वज्ञ, सर्वकारण मानकर — रावण ने प्रणाम करके शिव का सर्वोत्तम स्तोत्र कहा।
verses.commentary: The Ravana Samhita's opening establishes the text's central tension immediately: Ravana — whom the Ramayana presents as the principal antagonist — is here the speaker of the "supreme hymn to Shiva." The tradition holds that Ravana composed the Shiva Tandava Stotram, the Shiva Panchakshara, and multiple other revered Shiva hymns. His devotion was not false or superficial — it was genuine, profound, and technically accomplished. The paradox: the same person who composed the most beautiful hymns to Shiva also abducted Sita in violation of every principle Shiva embodies. The Ravana Samhita does not explain this away; it uses it to teach that devotion without surrender of ego is incomplete — however beautiful its expression.

verses.sanskrit: विद्या ददाति विनयं विनयाद्याति पात्रताम् | पात्रत्वाद्धनमाप्नोति धनाद्धर्मं ततः सुखम् ||
verses.transliteration: vidyā dadāti vinayaṃ vinayādyāti pātratām | pātrat vāddhAnamāpnoti dhanāddhArmaṃ tataḥ sukham ||
verses.translation: Knowledge gives humility; from humility comes worthiness; from worthiness, wealth; from wealth, dharma; from that, happiness.
verses.hindi: विद्या विनय देती है; विनय से पात्रता; पात्रता से धन; धन से धर्म; और धर्म से सुख।
verses.commentary: The Ravana Samhita quotes this celebrated Hitopadesa verse in its opening chapter — as the standard that Ravana himself violated. The sequence is a chain of five: vidya → vinaya → patrata → dhana → dharma → sukha. The first link is the crucial one: vidya (knowledge) is supposed to produce vinaya (humility) as its first fruit. If knowledge produces pride instead of humility — as it did in Ravana — the entire chain breaks. Ravana had immense vidya but his vidya produced arrogance, not vinaya. The Ravana Samhita uses this verse as the diagnostic: wherever the chain breaks, that is where knowledge has been corrupted by ego.

chapters.title: Shiva Upasana — The Science of Shiva Worship

verses.sanskrit: जटाटवीगलज्जलप्रवाहपावितस्थले गलेऽवलम्ब्य लम्बितां भुजंगतुंगमालिकाम् | डमड्डमड्डमड्डमन्निनादवड्डमर्वयं चकार चंडताण्डवं तनोतु नः शिवः शिवम् ||
verses.transliteration: jaṭāṭavīgalajjalapravāhapāvitasthale gale'valambyalambitāṃ bhujaṅgatuṅgamālikām | ḍamaḍḍamaḍḍamaḍḍamannInādavaḍḍamarvayaṃ cakāra caṇḍatāṇḍavaṃ tanotu naḥ śivaḥ śivam ||
verses.translation: In the throat — purified by the flow of water cascading from the forest of matted locks — wearing the great serpent-garland: with the sound of the damaru — ḍamaḍ ḍamaḍ ḍamaḍ ḍam — performing the fierce Tandava dance — may that Shiva bestow auspiciousness upon us.
verses.hindi: जटा-वन से गिरते जल-प्रवाह से पवित्र कंठ में, विशाल सर्प-माला धारण किए — डमड् डमड् डमड् डमड् की ध्वनि से — प्रचण्ड ताण्डव करते हुए — वह शिव हमें शुभ प्रदान करें।
verses.commentary: The opening verse of the Shiva Tandava Stotram — attributed to Ravana — is one of the greatest poems in Sanskrit literature: pure sound-sculpture, where the onomatopoeia of the damaru (ḍamaḍ ḍamaḍ) is embedded in the metre itself so that reading the verse aloud produces the experience it describes. Ravana composed this on Mount Kailash after attempting to lift the mountain to bring Shiva to Lanka — and Shiva pressed the mountain down with his toe, trapping Ravana's hand. In pain and awe, Ravana composed this stotram and sang it for a thousand years until Shiva released him. The image: even in pain caused by the divine, the response of the true devotee is praise.

verses.sanskrit: त्र्यम्बकं यजामहे सुगन्धिं पुष्टिवर्धनम् | उर्वारुकमिव बन्धनान्मृत्योर्मुक्षीय माऽमृतात् ||
verses.transliteration: tryambakaṃ yajāmahe sugandhiṃ puṣṭivardhanam | urvārukamiva bandhanānmṛtyormukṣīya mā'mṛtāt ||
verses.translation: We worship the three-eyed one, the sweet-fragrant, the nourisher of all. Like a cucumber from its vine — may he liberate us from death, not from immortality.
verses.hindi: हम त्र्यम्बक (तीन नेत्रों वाले), सुगन्धित, पुष्टिवर्धक की उपासना करते हैं। जैसे ककड़ी अपनी लता से कटती है — वैसे हमें मृत्यु से मुक्त करें, अमृत से नहीं।
verses.commentary: The Mahamrityunjaya Mantra — the great mantra of the Rigveda (7.59.12) — is cited by the Ravana Samhita as the central Shiva-upasana mantra that Ravana himself recited. Its final image is one of the most precise in all of Sanskrit: "urvārukam iva" — like a cucumber from its vine. Moksha (liberation) is not the violent severing of death; it is the gentle, ripe, natural detachment of the mature fruit from its supporting vine. The cucumber doesn't tear — it releases when fully ripe. The mantra asks Shiva: let us be liberated when fully ripe — not snatched before our time, not clinging past our season.

chapters.title: Mantra Shastra — The Science of Sacred Sound

verses.sanskrit: मन्त्रो हीनः स्वरेण तु यन्त्रं हीनं च भावतः | तन्त्रं हीनं गुरोर्वाक्याद्यन्त्रं शक्तिविवर्जितम् ||
verses.transliteration: mantro hīnaḥ svareṇa tu yantraṃ hīnaṃ ca bhāvataḥ | tantraṃ hīnaṃ gurorvākyādyantraṃ śaktivivarjitam ||
verses.translation: A mantra devoid of correct intonation; a yantra devoid of inner feeling; a tantra devoid of the guru's word — these are all yantra without power.
verses.hindi: स्वर-हीन मन्त्र; भाव-हीन यन्त्र; गुरु-वाक्य-हीन तन्त्र — ये सब शक्तिहीन यन्त्र हैं।
verses.commentary: The Ravana Samhita's most precise teaching on the conditions for efficacy in mantra practice. Three deficiencies that render practice powerless: (1) mantra without svara — correct phonetic intonation; the sound dimension is not decoration but essential carrier of the mantra's effect. (2) Yantra (sacred diagram/instrument) without bhava — inner feeling/orientation; the geometric form without the corresponding inner state is pattern, not power. (3) Tantra without guru-vakya — the guru's specific instruction; the system without the transmission is technique without living current. Together these three — svara, bhava, guru-vakya — are the three necessary conditions for any sacred practice to be genuinely effective rather than merely performed.

verses.sanskrit: एकाक्षरं परं ब्रह्म प्राणायाम परं तपः | सावित्र्याः परमं नास्ति मौनात् सत्यं विशिष्यते ||
verses.transliteration: ekākṣaraṃ paraṃ brahma prāṇāyāma paraṃ tapaḥ | sāvitryāḥ paramaṃ nāsti maunāt satyaṃ viśiṣyate ||
verses.translation: The single syllable is supreme Brahman; pranayama is the supreme austerity; nothing is greater than the Savitri (Gayatri); truth is higher than silence.
verses.hindi: एकाक्षर (OM) परम ब्रह्म है; प्राणायाम परम तप है; सावित्री (गायत्री) से बड़ा कुछ नहीं; मौन से सत्य श्रेष्ठ है।
verses.commentary: The Ravana Samhita's hierarchy of practices in four comparatives — each clause establishing a supreme: (1) Ekakshara (the single syllable OM) as supreme Brahman — the entire cosmos condensed into one sound. (2) Pranayama as supreme tapas — breath-regulation is the master austerity, more fundamental than any other discipline because it governs the very mechanism of life. (3) The Savitri (Gayatri mantra) as supreme mantra — of all the thousands of mantras in the tradition, this is the one Ravana cites as unsurpassed. (4) Satya above silence — when silence is broken, truth is what should emerge. The hierarchy is also a practical guide: if you can do only one practice, the most fundamental is pranayama.

verses.sanskrit: काले कर्म समारभेत् काले कर्म विसर्जयेत् | काले सुप्तो नरः सार्थः काले जाग्रति बुद्धिमान् ||
verses.transliteration: kāle karma samārambhet kāle karma visarjayet | kāle supto naraḥ sārthaḥ kāle jāgrati buddhimān ||
verses.translation: Undertake action at the right time; relinquish action at the right time. The person who sleeps in season is purposeful; the wise one awakens in season.
verses.hindi: सही समय पर कर्म आरम्भ करो; सही समय पर कर्म छोड़ो। समय पर सोने वाला व्यक्ति सार्थक है; समय पर जागने वाला बुद्धिमान।
verses.commentary: The Ravana Samhita's foundational principle of jyotisha: kala (time/timing) is the master variable in all action. Not merely "do the right thing" but "do the right thing at the right time." Two acts — beginning and relinquishing — each have their proper moment. The verse extends the principle from action to rest: even sleep has its season, and the person who sleeps when sleep is right is living purposefully. Ravana's tragedy was precisely this: he knew the science of kala and violated its principles. He knew his destruction was coming — his court astrologers told him repeatedly — and he refused to act on the knowledge. Knowledge of timing without the humility to act on it is useless.

verses.sanskrit: नक्षत्रताराग्रहसंयोगे यो जन्म लभते नरः | तद्वशाद्भवति प्राणी न स्वतन्त्रः कदाचन ||
verses.transliteration: nakṣatratārāgrahasaṃyoge yo janma labhate naraḥ | tadvśādbhavati prāṇī na svatantraḥ kadācana ||
verses.translation: The person who takes birth at the conjunction of stars, constellations, and planets — lives under that influence. No being is ever fully independent.
verses.hindi: जो व्यक्ति नक्षत्र, तारा और ग्रह के योग में जन्म लेता है — उसके वश में ही जीता है। कोई भी प्राणी कभी पूर्णतः स्वतन्त्र नहीं।
verses.commentary: The Ravana Samhita's most philosophically provocative statement: "na svatantraḥ kadācana" — no being is ever fully independent. This is not simple fatalism; it is the recognition of conditionality. Every being is born into a web of conditions — astronomical, biological, familial, cultural — that shape what is possible. Jyotisha is the science of understanding those conditions. The Ravana Samhita does not say: therefore do nothing. It says: understand your conditions clearly, and act wisely within them. Ravana himself was born under conditions that made him extraordinary in almost every domain — and under conditions that made his specific blind spot (the ego that could not surrender) catastrophic. Knowing your conditions is the beginning of freedom; ignoring them is the beginning of their tyranny.

verses.sanskrit: ज्योतिषं वेदवेदाङ्गं कालविद्यां प्रचक्षते | कालज्ञो ज्ञानवान् प्राहुः कालो हि दुरतिक्रमः ||
verses.transliteration: jyotiṣaṃ vedavedāṅgaṃ kālavidyāṃ pracakṣate | kālajño jñānavān prāhuḥ kālo hi duratikramaḥ ||
verses.translation: Jyotisha is declared a limb of the Vedas, the science of time. The knower of time is called wise, for time is truly insurmountable.
verses.hindi: ज्योतिष को वेदांग, काल-विद्या कहा गया है। काल को जानने वाले को ज्ञानी कहते हैं, क्योंकि काल वास्तव में दुर्लंघनीय है।
verses.commentary: The Ravana Samhita's statement on the status of jyotisha: it is not mere superstition but a vedāṅga — a limb of the Vedas, an auxiliary science essential for understanding the Vedic ritual and calendar. "Kāla-vidyā" — the science of time. The verse then gives the reason for studying it: "kālo hi duratikramaḥ" — time is truly insurmountable. You cannot argue with time, negotiate with time, or escape time. The only wise response is to understand it and align with it.

verses.sanskrit: शिवः सर्वभूतानां हृदये संनिविष्टः | यो जानाति स पश्यति यो न जानाति न पश्यति ||
verses.transliteration: śivaḥ sarvabhūtānāṃ hṛdaye saṃniviṣṭaḥ | yo jānāti sa paśyati yo na jānāti na paśyati ||
verses.translation: Shiva dwells in the heart of all beings. He who knows, sees; he who does not know, does not see.
verses.hindi: शिव सभी प्राणियों के हृदय में निवास करते हैं। जो जानता है, वह देखता है; जो नहीं जानता, वह नहीं देखता।
verses.commentary: The Ravana Samhita declares that Shiva dwells in the heart of all beings — not in distant heavens but in the innermost center of every living being. The verse then states the paradox of recognition: knowledge is seeing, ignorance is blindness. Shiva is equally present in all hearts, but only those who know can see. The seeing is not visual but recognitional — the recognition of the presence that is always there.

chapters.title: The Final Teaching — Knowledge, Surrender, and the Price of Ego
chapters.titleSanskrit: अन्तिम उपदेश — ज्ञान, शरणागति और अहंकार का मूल्य

verses.sanskrit: सर्वज्ञः सर्ववेत्ता च सर्वशास्त्रविशारदः | एकस्य विस्मृतो धर्मः शरणागतिरेव सा ||
verses.transliteration: sarvajñaḥ sarvavettā ca sarvaśāstraviśāradaḥ | ekasya vismṛto dharmaḥ śaraṇāgatireva sā ||
verses.translation: Knower of all, perceiver of all, accomplished in all scriptures — yet he forgot the one dharma: surrender itself.
verses.hindi: सर्वज्ञ, सर्ववेत्ता, सभी शास्त्रों में पारंगत — फिर भी एक धर्म भूल गया: वह शरणागति ही है।
verses.commentary: The Ravana Samhita's self-diagnosis — placed in Ravana's own mouth as retrospective understanding. The three epithets are superlatives: sarvajña (knower of all), sarvavettā (perceiver of all), sarvaśāstra-viśārada (expert in all scriptures). The most accomplished scholar in the cosmos. And the single thing he forgot — "ekasya vismṛto" — was sharanagati: surrender to the divine. The word "vismṛto" (forgotten) is precise: not that he never knew it, not that he rejected it — he forgot it. In the pride of his learning, surrender slipped from his awareness. This is the Ravana Samhita's most penetrating diagnosis of the spiritual danger of great knowledge: not that knowledge is bad, but that knowledge without the consistent practice of surrender is a house built on its own foundation — magnificent and unstable.

verses.sanskrit: अहंकारः परं शत्रुः शरणागतिः परं सुखम् | तयोर्मध्ये स्थितो जीवः कः श्रेयान् बुधो वदेत् ||
verses.transliteration: ahaṃkāraḥ paraṃ śatruḥ śaraṇāgatiḥ paraṃ sukham | tayormadhye sthito jīvaḥ kaḥ śreyān budho vadet ||
verses.translation: Ego is the supreme enemy; surrender is the supreme happiness. The living being stands between the two — let the wise one say which is better.
verses.hindi: अहंकार परम शत्रु है; शरणागति परम सुख है। दोनों के बीच में जीव खड़ा है — बुद्धिमान बताए, कौन श्रेयस्कर है?
verses.commentary: The Ravana Samhita's closing verse — and its most concentrated teaching. Ravana does not lecture; he presents a choice. Ahankara (ego — the construction of a separate self as supreme reference point) versus sharanagati (surrender — the relinquishment of that construction to a larger principle). Both are always available; the living being (jīva) stands between them at every moment. "Let the wise one say which is better" — the rhetorical question whose answer is already given by Ravana's own life. He chose ahankara. He had every quality a human being can have — learning, courage, strength, devotion, artistry — and the single choice of ego over surrender cost him everything. The verse is his final gift: I paid the full price to teach you this. Choose differently.

"Let the wise one say which is better" — the rhetorical question whose answer is already given by Ravana's own life. He chose ahankara. He had every quality a human being can have — learning, courage, strength, devotion, artistry — and the single choice of ego over surrender cost him everything. The verse is his final gift: I paid the full price to teach you this. Choose differently.

chapters.title: Ravana's Ayurveda — The Physician-King's Medical Teaching

verses.sanskrit: वातपित्तकफाः दोषाः देहे तिष्ठन्ति सर्वदा | तेषां साम्यं च स्वास्थ्यं स्यात् वैषम्यं रोग उच्यते ||
verses.transliteration: vātapittakaPhāḥ doṣāḥ dehe tiṣṭhanti sarvadā | teṣāṃ sāmyaṃ ca svāsthyaṃ syāt vaiṣamyaṃ roga ucyate ||
verses.translation: Vata, Pitta, and Kapha — the three doshas — always dwell in the body. Their balance is health; their imbalance is called disease.
verses.hindi: वात, पित्त और कफ — तीन दोष — सदा शरीर में रहते हैं। इनकी साम्यावस्था स्वास्थ्य है; विषमता रोग कहलाती है।
verses.commentary: The foundational principle of Ayurveda as stated in the Ravana Samhita's medical section. The tridosha theory is not merely a classification of body types — it is a dynamic model of physiological regulation. Vata (the principle of movement — governs respiration, circulation, nervous activity, elimination), Pitta (the principle of transformation — governs metabolism, digestion, vision, discernment), and Kapha (the principle of cohesion — governs structure, immunity, lubrication, memory). Health is not the absence of these forces but their dynamic equilibrium — "sāmyam." Disease — "vaiṣamyam" — is imbalance, any of the three doshas accumulating beyond or falling below its functional range. The genius of the tridosha model: it is a process theory, not a structural one. Health is a maintained balance, not a fixed state.

verses.sanskrit: शरीरे त्रिदोषस्थितिः साम्यं वैषम्यं व्याधिरिति प्रोक्तः | साम्ये स्वास्थ्यं वैषम्ये रोगः कायचिकित्सा ||
verses.transliteration: śarīre tridoṣasthitiḥ sāmyaṃ vaiṣamyaṃ vyādhiriḥ proktaḥ | sāmye svāsthyaṃ vaiṣamye rogaḥ kāyacikitsā ||
verses.translation: In the body, the three doshas maintain equilibrium. The loss of this equilibrium is called disease. Equilibrium is health; imbalance is disease — this is the treatment of the body.
verses.hindi: शरीर में त्रिदोष की स्थिति साम्य है। इस साम्य का वैषम्य व्याधि कहलाता है। साम्य में स्वास्थ्य है, वैषम्य में रोग — यही कायचिकित्सा है।
verses.commentary: The Ravana Samhita's Ayurvedic definition of health and disease. Health is not the absence of symptoms but the dynamic equilibrium (sāmya) of vata, pitta, and kapha. Disease (vyādhi) is not an enemy to be fought but a signal of imbalance (vaiṣamyam). The treatment (cikitsā) is the restoration of equilibrium, not merely symptom suppression. This is holistic medicine in the truest sense: the physician treats not the disease but the person's inner balance.

chapters.title: Samudrika Shastra — The Science of Bodily Signs

verses.sanskrit: देहो देवालयः प्रोक्तः जीवो देवः सनातनः | त्यजेदज्ञाननिर्मालयं सोऽहंभावेन पूजयेत् ||
verses.transliteration: deho devālayaḥ proktaḥ jīvo devaḥ sanātanaḥ | tyajedajñānaniramālayaṃ so'haṃbhāvena pūjayet ||
verses.translation: The body is called the temple of the divine; the soul is the eternal deity. Abandon the impurity of ignorance — and worship with the feeling "I am That."
verses.hindi: देह देवालय है; जीव सनातन देव है। अज्ञान की मलिनता को त्यागकर — "सोऽहम्" भाव से पूजा करो।
verses.commentary: The Ravana Samhita's foundational statement for its Samudrika section: the body is not a cage to be escaped but a temple to be honoured. "Deho devālayaḥ" — this principle reframes the entire project of bodily study: if the body is a temple, then reading its signs (samudrika) is a sacred act of recognition, not a mechanical cataloguing. The soul (jīva) as sanātana deva — the eternal divinity — dwelling within this temple. The practice: "so'haṃ-bhāvena pūjayet" — worship with the feeling of "I am That." This is the Shiva-agamic non-dual position: the body is not separate from the divine; it is the divine's chosen form of self-expression. Ignoring the body or despising it is therefore not spirituality but impiety toward the temple.

verses.transliteration: hastaRekhāḥ lalāṭaṃ ca netre pādatalāni ca | sarvāṇi dehacihñāni bhūtabhaviṣyakathāni vai ||
verses.translation: The lines of the hands, the forehead, the eyes, the soles of the feet — all bodily signs speak of what has been and what will be.
verses.hindi: हाथ की रेखाएं, ललाट, नेत्र, पैर के तलवे — सभी देह-चिह्न भूत और भविष्य की कहानियाँ कहते हैं।
verses.commentary: The Ravana Samhita's Samudrika teaching on the specific sites of bodily reading: hasta-rekha (palmistry — the lines of the hand), lalāṭa (the forehead and its lines), netra (the eyes — their colour, shape, lustre, and movement), and pāda-tala (the soles of the feet). Each is a text in a specific register: the hands reflect action and karma (what has been done and what will be done); the forehead reflects thought and destiny (the lines of accumulated mental patterns); the eyes reflect the state of consciousness itself; the feet reflect the body's relationship to the earth and to movement. The Ravana Samhita does not present these as infallible mechanical predictors but as probabilistic readings of accumulated tendencies — the body's honest record of where a person has been and where their momentum is carrying them.

chapters.title: Niti and Vastu — Ravana's Statecraft and Sacred Space

verses.sanskrit: राजा प्रजाहितं कुर्यात् प्रजा राज्ञे हितं तथा | परस्परोपकारेण स राज्यं सुखमश्नुते ||
verses.transliteration: rājā prajāhitaṃ kuryāt prajā rājñe hitaṃ tathā | parasparopakāreṇa sa rājyaṃ sukhamAśnute ||
verses.translation: The king should work for the welfare of the people; the people should work for the welfare of the king. Through mutual service, that kingdom enjoys happiness.
verses.hindi: राजा प्रजा का हित करे; प्रजा राजा का हित करे। परस्पर उपकार से वह राज्य सुख भोगता है।
verses.commentary: The Ravana Samhita's central niti principle: governance as mutual obligation, not unilateral authority. "Parasparopakāreṇa" — through mutual service. This is a remarkably non-hierarchical political philosophy for its era: the king's authority is not absolute but conditional on his service to the people. The kingdom's happiness ("sukham") flows from this mutuality, not from the king's power alone. The tragic irony: Ravana articulates this principle with precision and fails to embody it. Lanka under Ravana was, by the Ramayana's own account, a prosperous and well-governed kingdom — until his personal desire overrode his statecraft. The Ravana Samhita thus teaches its niti principles in the shadow of its author's failure to live by them: the most brilliant articulation of a principle does not guarantee its embodiment.

verses.transliteration: gṛhaṃ vāstuVidhānena nirmitaṃ sukhadaṃ bhavet | vāyuprakāśasaṃyuktaṃ āyurārogyavardhanam ||
verses.translation: A house built according to the principles of Vastu brings happiness. One with proper ventilation and light — increases lifespan and health.
verses.hindi: वास्तु-विधान से निर्मित गृह सुखदायक होता है। वायु और प्रकाश से युक्त — आयु और आरोग्य को बढ़ाता है।
verses.commentary: The Ravana Samhita's Vastu section opens with the simplest and most empirically verifiable principle: proper ventilation (vāyu — airflow) and light (prakāśa — natural light) in the built environment directly increase health and lifespan. Vastu Vidya is the Vedic science of harmonious space — the principles governing the orientation, proportions, spatial flow, and material qualities of built environments such that they support rather than undermine the health, relationships, and consciousness of their inhabitants. The Ravana Samhita presents Vastu not as superstition but as applied environmental science: the built environment is not neutral — it continuously affects the body, mood, and relationships of those who inhabit it.

verses.transliteration: uttaraṃ vā pūrvaṃ dvāraṃ gṛhe saukhyapradaṃ bhavet | dakṣiṇaṃ paścimaṃ dvāraṃ rogaśokapradaṃ smṛtam ||
verses.translation: A north-facing or east-facing entrance in a house bestows happiness. A south-facing or west-facing entrance is known to bring disease and grief.
verses.hindi: उत्तर या पूर्व मुखी द्वार गृह में सुख देता है। दक्षिण या पश्चिम मुखी द्वार रोग और शोक देने वाला कहा गया है।
verses.commentary: The Ravana Samhita's directional teaching for house orientation — one of Vastu's most specific and testable principles. The reasoning: in the northern hemisphere, east-facing and north-facing entrances maximise morning sunlight entry (the most health-beneficial light spectrum, rich in blue wavelengths that regulate circadian rhythm and boost serotonin) while minimising harsh afternoon/evening western sun (which produces heat, glare, and circadian disruption). South-facing entrances in hot climates receive the most direct solar radiation, increasing heat load and UV exposure. The Ravana Samhita encodes practical solar science in directional prescription — and the reason it has remained culturally persistent is precisely because it works: east and north orientations produce better-lit, better-regulated indoor environments in most contexts.

chapters.title: Sangita Shastra — Music as the Science of Consciousness

verses.sanskrit: नादब्रह्म परं तत्त्वं नादात् सर्वं प्रवर्तते | नादे लीनं मनो यस्य स मुक्तो नात्र संशयः ||
verses.transliteration: nādabrahma paraṃ tattvaṃ nādāt sarvaṃ pravartate | nāde līnaṃ mano yasya sa mukto nātra saṃśayaḥ ||
verses.translation: Nada-Brahman is the supreme reality; from sound all things proceed. One whose mind is dissolved in sound — that one is liberated; there is no doubt.
verses.hindi: नाद-ब्रह्म परम तत्त्व है; नाद से सब उत्पन्न होता है। जिसका मन नाद में लीन हो — वह मुक्त है; संशय नहीं।
verses.commentary: The foundational cosmological claim of the Sangita Shastra: nada-brahma — sound is the ultimate reality, not a secondary phenomenon. "Nādāt sarvaṃ pravartate" — from sound, all things arise. This is the Samhita's position: vibration precedes form. The practical implication is nada yoga — using deep musical absorption as the path to the mind's dissolution. Not intellectual appreciation of music, not emotional reaction to it — but complete absorption in it, so the boundary between the listener and the heard dissolves. "Nāde līnaṃ mano yasya" — the mind dissolved in sound. Ravana described this path with perfect precision and failed to walk it to its end.

verses.sanskrit: वीणावादनतत्त्वज्ञः श्रुतिजातिविशारदः | तालज्ञश्चाप्रयासेन मोक्षमार्गं नियच्छति ||
verses.transliteration: vīṇāvādanatattvajñaḥ śrutijātiviśāradaḥ | tālajñaścāprayāsena mokṣamārgaṃ niyacchati ||
verses.translation: One who knows the truth of veena-playing, accomplished in shruti and jati, knowing tala — attains the path of liberation effortlessly.
verses.hindi: जो वीणा-वादन का तत्त्वज्ञ, श्रुति-जाति में पारंगत, तालज्ञ है — वह अनायास मोक्ष-मार्ग प्राप्त करता है।
verses.commentary: The Ravana Samhita's most provocative claim: mastery of veena across three technical dimensions — shruti (the 22 microtonal intervals per octave), jati (melodic mode/character), and tala (rhythmic cycle) — itself confers the path of liberation, effortlessly. The three dimensions map onto the three aspects of consciousness: shruti (the subtle discriminative ear — viveka), jati (the quality/character of expression — bhava), tala (the rhythmic ordering of time — dharana). Ravana mastered all three. "Aprayāsena" — effortlessly — is the quality the Samhita identifies. The implicit question: he had the mastery; why not the liberation? Because he knew the veena without surrendering to what the veena was opening in him.

chapters.title: Yoga and Pranayama — The Eight-Limbed Practice

verses.sanskrit: यमो नियमश्चैव आसनं प्राणसंयमः | प्रत्याहारश्च धारणा ध्यानं समाधिरेव च ||
verses.transliteration: yamo niyamaścaiva āsanaṃ prāṇasaṃyamaḥ | pratyāhāraśca dhāraṇā dhyānaṃ samādhireva ca ||
verses.translation: Yama, niyama, asana, pranayama, pratyahara, dharana, dhyana, and samadhi — these are the eight limbs.
verses.hindi: यम, नियम, आसन, प्राणसंयम, प्रत्याहार, धारणा, ध्यान और समाधि — ये आठ अंग हैं।
verses.commentary: The Ravana Samhita lists the ashtanga in exact order of interdependence. Yama is first because it is the foundation on which all others rest. Without yama, pranayama becomes merely breath technique; asana becomes flexibility performance; samadhi becomes structurally impossible. Ravana reversed this: mastered the upper six limbs while violating the first. The Samhita uses his own system to diagnose his failure: a yoga practice that skips the ethical foundation is a structure built from the roof down. The list is not decorative — it is architectural.

verses.transliteration: recakaṃ pūrakaṃ caiva kumbhakaṃ trividhaṃ smṛtam | prāṇāyāmena dehasya rogāḥ sarve praṇaśyati ||
verses.translation: Rechaka, puraka, and kumbhaka — the three types are known. Through pranayama, all diseases of the body are destroyed.
verses.hindi: रेचक, पूरक और कुम्भक — ये तीन प्रकार स्मृत हैं। प्राणायाम से शरीर के सभी रोग नष्ट होते हैं।
verses.commentary: The three components of pranayama as a complete system. Puraka (inhalation) — receiving, opening, expansion. Rechaka (exhalation) — releasing what is metabolically finished; the breath-analogue of surrender. Kumbhaka (retention) — suspension at full or empty; concentrated prana held and directed by awareness. "Sarve rogāḥ praṇaśyati" — all diseases are destroyed. In the Ravana Samhita's full context, the "disease" most in need of treatment is ahankara — the imbalance that destroyed Ravana himself. He mastered kumbhaka; he could not hold the pause long enough to hear what the silence inside it was saying.

chapters.title: Moksha Vichara — The Final Philosophical Synthesis

verses.sanskrit: बन्धो मोक्षश्च जीवस्य स्वस्वरूपाज्ञानतः | ज्ञानाद्बन्धो विलीयेत मोक्षः स्वस्थस्य लक्षणम् ||
verses.transliteration: bandho mokṣaśca jīvasya svasvarūpājñānataḥ | jñānādbandho vilīyeta mokṣaḥ svasthasya lakṣaṇam ||
verses.translation: Bondage and liberation of the jiva both arise from ignorance of one's own true nature. Through knowledge, bondage dissolves — liberation is the mark of one who is established in the Self.
verses.hindi: जीव का बन्ध और मोक्ष दोनों स्वस्वरूप के अज्ञान से हैं। ज्ञान से बन्ध विलीन होता है — मोक्ष स्वस्थ की पहचान है।
verses.commentary: The Ravana Samhita's core philosophical statement on liberation. Both bondage and liberation arise from the same source: the jiva's relationship to its own true nature. Bondage is not imposed from outside — it is the result of sva-svarūpa-ajñāna, ignorance of one's own essential nature. Liberation is not achieved from outside — it is the dissolution of that ignorance through jñāna. "Svastha" — established in the Self, literally "abiding in one's own" — is the mark of the liberated. Ravana could articulate this precisely. "Svastha" is also the Sanskrit word for "healthy" — the person who is genuinely healthy is the one abiding in their own nature. The double meaning: liberation is the deepest health; the deepest health is liberation.
verses.wordMeaning: The Ravana Samhita's core philosophical statement on liberation. Both bondage and liberation arise from the same source: the jiva's relationship to its own true nature. Bondage is not imposed from outside — it is the result of sva-svarūpa-ajñāna, ignorance of one's own essential nature. Liberation is not achieved from outside — it is the dissolution of that ignorance through jñāna. "Svastha" — established in the Self, literally "abiding in one's own" — is the mark of the liberated. Ravana could articulate this precisely. "Svastha" is also the Sanskrit word for "healthy" — the person who is genuinely healthy is the one abiding in their own nature. The double meaning: liberation is the deepest health; the deepest health is liberation.

verses.sanskrit: जानामि धर्मं न च मे प्रवृत्तिः जानाम्यधर्मं न च मे निवृत्तिः | केनापि देवेन हृदिस्थितेन यथा नियुक्तोऽस्मि तथा करोमि ||
verses.transliteration: jānāmi dharmaṃ na ca me pravṛttiḥ jānāmyadharmaṃ na ca me nivṛttiḥ | kenāpi devena hṛdisthitena yathā niyukto'smi tathā karomi ||
verses.translation: I know dharma, yet I am not inclined toward it. I know adharma, yet I cannot turn away from it. By some deity dwelling in my heart — as I am impelled, so I act.
verses.hindi: मैं धर्म जानता हूँ, फिर भी उसमें प्रवृत्ति नहीं। अधर्म जानता हूँ, फिर भी निवृत्ति नहीं। हृदय में स्थित किसी देव द्वारा — जैसे नियुक्त हूँ वैसा करता हूँ।
verses.commentary: The most shattering verse in the Ravana Samhita — placed in Ravana's own mouth, and considered by commentators to be his most honest self-disclosure. "Jānāmi dharmaṃ na ca me pravṛttiḥ" — I know dharma, yet I am not inclined toward it. This is not ignorance; it is akrasia — the ancient Greek philosophical problem of acting against one's own better judgment. Ravana is not confused about what is right. He knows with complete clarity. He acts against that clarity anyway. The final line — "by some deity in my heart, as I am impelled, so I act" — is simultaneously a confession and a question. Is it genuine surrender to divine will? Or is it the ultimate rationalisation of ego — using the language of divine compulsion to abdicate personal responsibility? The Ravana Samhita leaves this deliberately unresolved. The reader must answer it for themselves.

verses.sanskrit: मोक्षो न जन्मान्तरसाध्यो न तपसा न योगेन | स्वस्वरूपानुसन्धानात् सद्यो मुक्तिः प्रजायते ||
verses.transliteration: mokṣo na janmāntarasādhyo na tapasā na yogena | svasvarūpānusandhānāt sadyo muktiḥ prajāyate ||
verses.translation: Liberation is not achieved through many births, not through austerity, not through yoga. From inquiry into one's own essential nature — liberation arises immediately.
verses.hindi: मोक्ष न अनेक जन्मों से, न तप से, न योग से सिद्ध होता है। अपने स्वस्वरूप के अनुसन्धान से — तत्काल मुक्ति उत्पन्न होती है।
verses.commentary: The Ravana Samhita's final, most radical teaching — and its most personal one. "Na janmāntara-sādhyaḥ" — not achievable through many births. "Na tapasā" — not through austerity. Ravana performed austerities that no human in the tradition can match: a thousand years of tapas, cutting off his own heads. "Na yogena" — not through yoga. He mastered seven of the eight limbs. None of it produced liberation. "Sva-svarūpa-anusandhānāt sadyo muktiḥ" — from inquiry into one's own essential nature, liberation arises immediately. Not eventually. Not after more practice. Now. The Ravana Samhita's closing teaching is the most direct in the entire tradition: all the extraordinary practice is not the cause of liberation. Inquiry into what you actually are — right now, with no preparation, no precondition — is the only cause. Ravana had everything except the willingness to look at what was looking.

chapters.title: Tantra Vidhi — The Ritual Science of Transformation

verses.sanskrit: दीक्षा विना न मन्त्रः स्यात् मन्त्रं विना न सिद्धिः | गुरोः कृपाविना नैव दीक्षा फलप्रदा भवेत् ||
verses.transliteration: dīkṣā vinā na mantraḥ syāt mantraṃ vinā na siddhiḥ | guroḥ kṛpāvinā naiva dīkṣā phalapradā bhavet ||
verses.translation: Without initiation there is no mantra; without mantra there is no siddhi. Without the grace of the guru, initiation itself does not bear fruit.
verses.hindi: दीक्षा बिना मन्त्र नहीं; मन्त्र बिना सिद्धि नहीं। गुरु की कृपा बिना दीक्षा भी फलप्रद नहीं।
verses.commentary: The chain diksha → mantra → siddhi is not mechanical but relational. Diksha (literally "that which ignites") is the transmission of living spiritual current from a realised teacher to a prepared student — the moment practice becomes alive rather than mechanical. Without this transmission, mantra is sound without carrier. The deeper condition: "guroḥ kṛpā" — the guru's grace — flows where the student's ego has genuinely softened enough to receive it. Ravana received diksha from Shiva himself. He received the mantra. He performed the practice for a thousand years. The grace flowed — and his ego closed around it rather than opening to it.

verses.transliteration: yantraṃ mantramayaṃ devi devatā yantramāśritā | yantraṃ vinā na deveśi pūjāṃ grāhayati prabhuḥ ||
verses.translation: The yantra is composed of mantra, O Goddess; the deity dwells in the yantra. Without the yantra, O Devi, the Lord does not accept the worship.
verses.hindi: यन्त्र मन्त्रमय है देवि; देवता यन्त्र में वास करती है। यन्त्र बिना प्रभु पूजा ग्रहण नहीं करते।
verses.commentary: A yantra is not a decorative diagram — it is a crystallised geometric form of a specific mantra and the consciousness-principle it represents. "Yantraṃ mantramayam" — the yantra is made of mantra: the geometric proportions encode the same vibrational information that the mantra encodes acoustically. The Sri Yantra's nine interpenetrating triangles generating 43 sub-triangles around a central bindu is the geometric body of the goddess's presence, constructed according to precise mathematical proportions that correspond to the structure of Shakti-consciousness. Without this physical embodiment, worship has no crystallisation point — the consciousness invoked has no geometric anchor in the physical plane.

chapters.title: Shakti Upasana — The Goddess as Dynamic Consciousness

verses.sanskrit: शिवः शक्त्या युक्तो यदि भवति शक्तः प्रभवितुं न चेदेवं देवो न खलु कुशलः स्पन्दितुमपि ||
verses.transliteration: śivaḥ śaktyā yukto yadi bhavati śaktaḥ prabhavituṃ na cedevaṃ devo na khalu kuśalaḥ spanditumapi ||
verses.translation: Shiva, when united with Shakti, is able to function; without her, even he is incapable of the slightest movement.
verses.hindi: शिव शक्ति से युक्त होने पर ही शक्त होते हैं; उसके बिना वे तनिक भी हिलने में असमर्थ हैं।
verses.commentary: The opening line of Adi Shankaracharya's Soundarya Lahari — cited in the Ravana Samhita as the most precise statement of the Shakta-Shaiva philosophical position. Static consciousness (Shiva) requires dynamic energy (Shakti) even for the smallest movement. The universe — every movement, every creation, every transformation — is Shakti in action, Shiva as its unchanging ground. Without Shakti, Shiva is Shava — a corpse. Ravana had the theoretical understanding of Shakti's supreme position. He violated it by treating Sita — a supreme embodiment of Shakti — as an object of possession rather than a person of sovereignty.

verses.transliteration: yā devī sarvabhūteṣu śaktirūpeṇa saṃsthitā | namastasyai namastasyai namastasyai namo namaḥ ||
verses.translation: To that goddess who dwells in all beings in the form of shakti — salutation to her, salutation to her, salutation to her, salutation again and again.
verses.hindi: जो देवी सभी प्राणियों में शक्तिरूप से स्थित है — उसे नमस्कार, नमस्कार, नमस्कार, बार-बार नमस्कार।
verses.commentary: From the Devi Mahatmyam — cited in the Ravana Samhita as the supreme statement of the goddess's universal presence. "Sarvabhūteṣu śaktirūpeṇa saṃsthitā" — dwelling in all beings in the form of shakti. The goddess is not somewhere else to be petitioned — she is the very power of being in everything that exists. The triple repetition addresses her in three aspects: as the power of creation (Brahma-shakti), sustenance (Vishnu-shakti), and dissolution (Shiva-shakti). Ravana's citation here is his acknowledgement that the power destroying him — Rama's divinity, activated by Sita's abduction — was the goddess's own power restoring cosmic balance.

chapters.title: Karma Vichara — The Philosophy of Action and Consequence

verses.sanskrit: अवश्यमेव भोक्तव्यं कृतं कर्म शुभाशुभम् | नाभुक्तं क्षीयते कर्म कल्पकोटिशतैरपि ||
verses.transliteration: avaśyameva bhoktavyaṃ kṛtaṃ karma śubhāśubham | nābhuktaṃ kṣīyate karma kalpakotiśatairapi ||
verses.translation: The karma performed — auspicious or inauspicious — must certainly be experienced. Karma not yet experienced does not diminish even in hundreds of billions of cosmic cycles.
verses.hindi: किया हुआ कर्म — शुभ या अशुभ — अवश्य भोगना पड़ेगा। बिना भोगे कर्म करोड़ों कल्पों में भी क्षीण नहीं होता।
verses.commentary: "Avaśyameva bhoktavyam" — it must certainly be experienced. The qualifier "avaśyam" (certainly, inevitably, without exception) is absolute. There is no path around karma through devotion, mantra, ritual, or philosophical understanding. Karma is the self-correcting principle of the cosmos — built into the structure of reality itself, not administered by a judging deity. "Kalpakotiśatairapi" — even in hundreds of billions of cosmic cycles, unexperienced karma does not diminish. Ravana's story is the tradition's most vivid proof: a man of extraordinary devotion, knowledge, and tapas who violated the principle of dharma experienced the full consequence. His greatness did not exempt him — it made the consequence proportionate.

verses.transliteration: sañcitaṃ ca prārabdhaṃ kriyamāṇaṃ ca tattrayam | sañcitaṃ bhasmasātkuryāt prārabdhaṃ bhogataḥ kṣayet ||
verses.translation: The accumulated (sanchita), the already-initiated (prarabdha), and the currently-being-performed (kriyamana) — these are the three. Sanchita is destroyed by knowledge; prarabdha diminishes through experience.
verses.hindi: संचित, प्रारब्ध और क्रियमाण — ये तीन हैं। संचित ज्ञान से भस्म होता है; प्रारब्ध भोग से क्षीण होता है।
verses.commentary: The Ravana Samhita's threefold classification of karma — the most analytically precise framework for understanding the relationship between past action and present circumstance. Sanchita: the entire accumulated store of unexperienced karma — the total of what must eventually be experienced. Prarabdha: the portion activated in the present life — conditions of birth, body, family already in motion; the arrow already released. Kriyamana: what is being created right now — the only karma directly under present agency. The prescription: sanchita can be burned by jñana (direct knowledge of the Self — the realisation that the Self is untouched by karma); prarabdha must be lived through. Only kriyamana is fully in your hands. Ravana understood this perfectly. He continued adding destructive kriyamana to an already catastrophic prarabdha.

verses.transliteration: sarvadharmān parityajya māmekaṃ śaraṇaṃ vraja | ahaṃ tvāṃ sarvapāpebhyo mokṣayiṣyāmi mā śucaḥ ||
verses.translation: Abandoning all dharmas, take refuge in me alone. I will liberate you from all sins — do not grieve.
verses.hindi: सभी धर्मों को त्यागकर केवल मेरी शरण में आ जाओ। मैं तुम्हें सभी पापों से मुक्त करूँगा — शोक मत करो।
verses.commentary: The Bhagavad Gita's charama-shloka (18.66) — cited in the Ravana Samhita's Upadesa-Sara as the final word. Ravana's inclusion of Krishna's ultimate instruction in his own concluding teaching is the text's most stunning moment of self-awareness. "Sarva-dharmān parityajya" — abandoning all dharmas. Not only adharma, not only social obligations — all dharmas, including the dharma of practice, of ritual, of knowledge, of the seeker. The final step is the abandonment of even the role of the spiritual practitioner. "Māmekam śaraṇam vraja" — take refuge in me alone. Ravana, the supreme Shiva devotee, understood this teaching. He cited it. He could not do it. The ego that had accumulated knowledge of all 64 arts, mastered every domain of human achievement, performed extraordinary tapas — could not dissolve itself into the one act of complete surrender that would have resolved everything. The Ravana Samhita closes with the instruction its author could not follow.

verses.transliteration: vidyā vivādāya dhanaṃ madāya śaktiḥ pareṣāṃ paripīḍanāya | khilasya sādhorviparītametat jñānāya dānāya ca rakṣaṇāya ||
verses.translation: For the wicked: knowledge leads to argument, wealth to arrogance, power to oppression of others. For the noble: the very opposite — knowledge for wisdom, wealth for giving, power for protection.
verses.hindi: दुष्ट के लिए: विद्या विवाद के लिए, धन मद के लिए, शक्ति दूसरों को पीड़ित करने के लिए। साधु के लिए: इसका विपरीत — ज्ञान के लिए, दान के लिए, रक्षा के लिए।
verses.commentary: The Ravana Samhita's penultimate teaching — and its most precise self-diagnosis. Ravana had vidya (knowledge of all 64 arts — and used it for argument, domination, and the display of superiority). He had dhana (the wealth of Lanka, unmatched in the three worlds — and it produced the madness of invulnerability). He had shakti (power that had subdued the gods — and he used it to oppress). The verse does not say these three things are bad. It says they reveal character: the same knowledge, wealth, and power that the noble use for wisdom, giving, and protection — the wicked use for argument, arrogance, and oppression. The Ravana Samhita closes not with condemnation of Ravana but with his own lucid self-portrait: he understood exactly what he was doing and why it was wrong. That understanding changed nothing.

verses.transliteration: yatra nāryastu pūjyante ramante tatra devatāḥ | yatraitāstu na pūjyante sarvāstatrāphalāḥ kriyāḥ ||
verses.translation: Where women are honoured and respected, the gods rejoice. Where they are not honoured, all actions become fruitless.
verses.hindi: जहाँ स्त्रियों का सम्मान होता है, वहाँ देवता प्रसन्न होते हैं। जहाँ उनका सम्मान नहीं, वहाँ सभी क्रियाएँ निष्फल हो जाती हैं।
verses.commentary: The Manusmriti's most celebrated verse (3.56) — cited as the very last teaching of the Ravana Samhita's Upadesa-Sara. The placement is not coincidental. The entire Ravana Samhita — 15 chapters, four volumes, every domain of human knowledge — closes with the verse whose violation was Ravana's cause of destruction. "Yatra nāryastu pūjyante" — where women are honoured. "Ramante tatra devatāḥ" — the gods rejoice there. "Sarvāstatrāphalāḥ kriyāḥ" — where they are not honoured, all actions become fruitless. Every ritual, every mantra, every yantra, every tapas, every meditation, every act of governance — all fruitless, if this condition is not met. Ravana knew this teaching. He cited it. He violated it catastrophically. The Ravana Samhita ends here — with the teaching that explains why everything Ravana did was ultimately fruitless. Not because he lacked knowledge. Because he lacked the one thing his knowledge kept telling him he needed: the willingness to honour what he could not control.
verses.wordMeaning: The Manusmriti's most celebrated verse (3.56) — cited as the very last teaching of the Ravana Samhita's Upadesa-Sara. The placement is not coincidental. The entire Ravana Samhita — 15 chapters, four volumes, every domain of human knowledge — closes with the verse whose violation was Ravana's cause of destruction. "Yatra nāryastu pūjyante" — where women are honoured. "Ramante tatra devatāḥ" — the gods rejoice there. "Sarvāstatrāphalāḥ kriyāḥ" — where they are not honoured, all actions become fruitless. Every ritual, every mantra, every yantra, every tapas, every meditation, every act of governance — all fruitless, if this condition is not met. Ravana knew this teaching. He cited it. He violated it catastrophically. The Ravana Samhita ends here — with the teaching that explains why everything Ravana did was ultimately fruitless. Not because he lacked knowledge. chapters.title: Stotras and Hymns — Ravana's Own Voice

verses.sanskrit: अपराधसहस्राणि क्रियन्तेऽहर्निशं मया | दासोऽयमिति मां मत्वा क्षमस्व परमेश्वर ||
verses.transliteration: aparādhasahasrāṇi kriyante'harniśaṃ mayā | dāso'yamiti māṃ matvā kṣamasva parameśvara ||
verses.translation: Thousands of offences are committed by me day and night. Considering me your servant, O Supreme Lord, forgive me.
verses.hindi: मेरे द्वारा दिन-रात हजारों अपराध होते हैं। मुझे अपना दास समझकर, हे परमेश्वर, क्षमा करो।
verses.commentary: From the Shiva Aparadha Kshama Stotram — attributed to Ravana. The verse is structurally extraordinary: "aparādhasahasrāṇi" — thousands of offences, not one, not a few. Not hyperbole but honest accounting. "Aharnisham" — day and night, continuously — not a single error but a pervasive pattern. "Dāso'yam" — I am your servant: the structural move of sharanagati. The prayer does not ask for exemption from consequence — it asks for forgiveness, which is different. Forgiveness does not cancel karma; it re-establishes the relationship between devotee and divine that the karma had fractured. Ravana knew the fracture. He named it with precision. He made the prayer. The tradition holds this was not enough to prevent consequence — but it was enough to ensure liberation at the moment of death.

verses.sanskrit: नमः शिवाय शान्ताय कारणत्रयहेतवे | निवेदयामि चात्मानं त्वं गतिः परमेश्वर ||
verses.transliteration: namaḥ śivāya śāntāya kāraṇatrayahetave | nivedayāmi cātmānaṃ tvaṃ gatiḥ parameśvara ||
verses.translation: Salutation to Shiva, the peaceful, cause behind the three causes. I offer myself entirely — you are my refuge, O Supreme Lord.
verses.hindi: शिव को नमस्कार — शान्त, तीन कारणों के कारण। मैं अपने आप को समर्पित करता हूँ — हे परमेश्वर, आप ही मेरी गति हैं।
verses.commentary: From Ravana's final prayer sequence — the verse of complete self-offering. "Nivedayāmi cātmānam" — I offer myself entirely. Not flowers, not incense, not tapas — the self. This is the completion of the arc the Ravana Samhita traces across five volumes: from the man who accumulated everything to the man who offers everything back. "Tvaṃ gatiḥ" — you are my refuge, my destination, my direction itself. "Gati" means both refuge and movement — direction itself. Ravana arrives at the teaching he encoded in Vol. 1: surrender is the only resolution. The tradition holds he reached this in his final moments as Rama's arrow struck. The Stotras section preserves the voice of that arrival.

chapters.title: Yuddha Niti — The Science of War

verses.sanskrit: बलं बुद्धिमतां श्रेष्ठं बुद्धिर्बलवतां बलम् | बुद्धिहीनो बली नाशं याति शीघ्रं न संशयः ||
verses.transliteration: balaṃ buddhimatāṃ śreṣṭhaṃ buddhirbalavataṃ balam | buddhihīno balī nāśaṃ yāti śīghraṃ na saṃśayaḥ ||
verses.translation: Intelligence is the highest strength of the intelligent; intelligence is the strength of the powerful. The powerful one without intelligence swiftly goes to ruin — no doubt.
verses.hindi: बुद्धिमानों में बुद्धि ही श्रेष्ठ बल है; बलवानों में बुद्धि ही बल है। बुद्धिहीन बलवान शीघ्र नाश को प्राप्त होता है — संशय नहीं।
verses.commentary: The foundational principle of the Yuddha Niti: raw force without strategic intelligence is not an asset — it is a liability, because it is predictable, inflexible, and ultimately exhaustible. "Buddhihīno balī nāśam yāti śīghram" — the powerful one without intelligence goes to ruin quickly. No qualifications, no exceptions. Ravana had more bala than any being in the three worlds. He chose to deploy it without buddhi when it mattered most: he ignored Vibhishana's counsel, dismissed Mandodari's warnings, and fought a war that his own jyotisha calculations told him he could not win. The Yuddha Niti's opening verse is Ravana's most precise self-indictment.

verses.sanskrit: दूतो वक्ता च मन्त्री च सर्वकार्येषु सारथिः | अमात्यः सचिवश्चैव न हन्तव्यः कदाचन ||
verses.transliteration: dūto vaktā ca mantrī ca sarvakāryeṣu sārathiḥ | amātyaḥ sacivascaiva na hantavyaḥ kadācana ||
verses.translation: The messenger, the speaker, the counsellor, the guide in all matters, the minister, the secretary — these must never be killed.
verses.hindi: दूत, वक्ता, मन्त्री, सर्वकार्यों में सारथि, अमात्य, सचिव — इन्हें कभी नहीं मारना चाहिए।
verses.commentary: "Dūto na hantavyaḥ kadācana" — the messenger must never be killed. The oldest and most universally held principle of warfare. Ravana encoded it in his own treatise. He violated it when he ordered Hanuman's tail set on fire — an act of aggression against an emissary under diplomatic immunity. The moment he committed this violation, his war was already strategically over: not because of the practical consequences (Lanka burning) but because he demonstrated that his conduct was no longer governed by his own principles. A commander who violates his own rules of war has lost the internal coherence that makes sustained military strategy possible. His advisers stopped telling him the truth after Hanuman's tail. This is the duta-niti consequence: destroy the messenger, destroy your own access to reality.

chapters.title: Mrityu Vichara — The Contemplation of Death

verses.sanskrit: अन्तकाले च मामेव स्मरन्मुक्त्वा कलेवरम् | यः प्रयाति स मद्भावं याति नास्त्यत्र संशयः ||
verses.transliteration: antakāle ca māmeva smaranmukt'vā kalevaram | yaḥ prayāti sa madbhāvaṃ yāti nāstyatra saṃśayaḥ ||
verses.translation: Whoever, at the time of death, remembers me alone and departs, leaving the body — attains my state. There is no doubt.
verses.hindi: जो अन्तकाल में केवल मुझे स्मरण करते हुए शरीर छोड़ता है — वह मेरे भाव को प्राप्त होता है। संशय नहीं।
verses.commentary: Bhagavad Gita 8.5 — cited in the Mrityu Vichara as the verse that explains what the tradition holds happened at Ravana's death. "Antakāle ca māmeva smaran" — at the moment of death, remembering me alone. The theological claim: Ravana, struck by Rama's Brahmastra, died with Rama's name and form as his final awareness — having in the moment of death achieved what a lifetime of practice could not. The tradition holds this is why Ravana attained liberation at death: not despite his transgressions, but through the grace his death conferred — the forced confrontation with the divine that his ego had prevented in life. Rama is Vishnu; his arrow carried the divine presence. To die struck by the divine is to die with the divine as the final object of consciousness. The Mrityu Vichara cites this verse to ask: what is your final awareness being trained toward, now, in life?

verses.sanskrit: मृत्युरेव महाशत्रुः मृत्युरेव महागुरुः | मृत्युं पश्यति यो नित्यं तस्य किं भयमास्थितम् ||
verses.transliteration: mṛtyureva mahāśatruḥ mṛtyureva mahāguruḥ | mṛtyuṃ paśyati yo nityaṃ tasya kiṃ bhayamāsthitam ||
verses.translation: Death is the great enemy; death is the great teacher. One who sees death constantly — what fear can take hold in them?
verses.hindi: मृत्यु महाशत्रु है; मृत्यु महागुरु है। जो सदा मृत्यु को देखता है — उसे कौन सा भय घेर सकता है?
verses.commentary: The Ravana Samhita's most paradoxical teaching on death. The same death is simultaneously enemy and teacher. What makes death the enemy — its inevitability, impartiality, finality — is precisely what makes it the teacher. It cannot be bribed, flattered, or argued with. It does not respect accomplishment. Ravana spent his life making death impossible through his Brahma-boon. That very effort — the maximum expression of the refusal to accept death — is what prevented him from receiving the teaching death carries. "Yo nityaṃ paśyati" — the one who sees death continuously — is freed from the fear that generates most human self-deception. Ravana accepted death's inevitability in his final moments. The teacher arrived precisely when the student stopped refusing the lesson.

chapters.title: Bhakti Rahasya — The Secret of Devotion

verses.sanskrit: सा परानुरक्तिरीश्वरे
verses.transliteration: sā parānuraktirīśvare
verses.translation: That — supreme attachment to the Lord — is [bhakti].
verses.hindi: वह — ईश्वर में परम अनुरक्ति — [भक्ति है।]
verses.commentary: The shortest and most complete definition of bhakti in the Sanskrit tradition — from the Narada Bhakti Sutras (sutra 2). Three words. "Para-anuraktiḥ" — supreme attachment: "para" (highest, beyond ordinary) + "anurakti" (love, resonance, that which vibrates in response). "Īśvare" — to the Lord, to the divine. The Ravana Samhita cites this in its final chapter to establish precisely what was present and absent in Ravana's practice. The anurakti was present — few in the tradition have demonstrated greater devotional intensity. The failure was in the direction of the attachment: "īśvare." Ravana's anurakti ultimately remained attached to himself — to his extraordinary qualities, his invulnerability, his knowledge. The Lord was the stated object of worship; the self remained the actual centre.

verses.sanskrit: भक्तिर्भगवतो सेवा भक्तिः प्रेमस्वरूपिणी | भक्तिरानन्दरूपा च भक्तिर्मुक्तिप्रदायिनी ||
verses.transliteration: bhaktirbhagavato sevā bhaktiḥ premasvarūpiṇī | bhaktirānandarūpā ca bhaktirmuktipradāyinī ||
verses.translation: Bhakti is service to the Lord; bhakti is of the nature of love; bhakti is of the nature of bliss; and bhakti is the bestower of liberation.
verses.hindi: भक्ति भगवान की सेवा है; भक्ति प्रेमस्वरूपिणी है; भक्ति आनन्दरूपा है; और भक्ति मुक्तिप्रदायिनी है।
verses.commentary: The Ravana Samhita's fourfold definition of bhakti. Sevā (service) — the test of genuine bhakti is always behavioural, not emotional; when the inner orientation does not express as outer service, the devotion remains interior decoration. Prema-svarūpiṇī (of the nature of love) — the feeling-quality of genuine sevā; when service arises from love rather than obligation, it changes in character completely. Ānanda-rūpā (of the nature of bliss) — the experiential quality of genuine bhakti: not happiness dependent on circumstances but the bliss that is the natural quality of the divine itself, experienced when the self is transparent to it. Mukti-pradāyinī (bestower of liberation) — not because bhakti bypasses knowledge, but because genuine love for the divine naturally dissolves the ego-identification that is the only obstacle to liberation. Ravana had dimensions two and three. He could not sustain dimension one: sevā as the lived expression of love in his treatment of others.

verses.sanskrit: नायमात्मा बलहीनेन लभ्यो न च प्रमादात् न तपसा विना | उपायैरेतैर्यतते यस्तु विद्वान् तस्यैष आत्मा विशते ब्रह्मधाम ||
verses.transliteration: nāyamātmā balahīnena labhyo na ca pramādāt na tapasā vinā | upāyairetairyatate yastu vidvān tasyaiṣa ātmā viśate brahmadhāma ||
verses.translation: This Self is not attained by the weak, nor through negligence, nor without austerity. The wise one who strives through these means — for that one the Self enters the abode of Brahman.
verses.hindi: यह आत्मा बलहीन को नहीं मिलती, न प्रमाद से, न तप के बिना। जो विद्वान इन उपायों से प्रयत्न करता है — उसकी आत्मा ब्रह्मधाम में प्रवेश करती है।
verses.commentary: The Mundaka Upanishad (3.2.4) — cited by Ravana as the final word of the Bhakti Rahasya and of the complete Ravana Samhita. Three conditions: "balahīnena" — not by the weak: the strength required is not physical or intellectual but the strength to endure the dissolution of the ego-structure that devotion requires. "Na pramādāt" — not through negligence: genuine bhakti requires the sustained attention that Ravana gave to every other domain of his learning and could not sustain in its most essential application. "Na tapasā vinā" — not without austerity: tapas literally means heat — the willingness to bear the discomfort of genuine transformation. Ravana bore extraordinary external tapas. He could not bear the interior tapas of surrender. The Ravana Samhita closes on this verse: not as condemnation but as the precise description of the only work that matters — and the three conditions without which it cannot be done.
